prompt: In `Fine.java`'s stack trace, which line names the first method of the program's own code?
hint: Skip the lines that start with `java.base/`.

choices.text: `at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:565)`
choices.why: That is inside the JDK's `Integer` class, whose source you did not write.

choices.text: `at Fine.daysLate(Fine.java:6)`
choices.why: Right: the call to `parseInt`, and the place to start reading.

choices.text: `at Fine.main(Fine.java:15)`
choices.why: That is the program's code too, but the last frame, not the first.

prompt: `Fine.java` printed `150` and then a stack trace. Why was `done` never printed?
hint: Where was the exception caught?

choices.text: Because `println` skips its line after an error
choices.why: `println` was never reached; the exception left `main` first.

choices.text: Because `parseInt` returned 0 and the program stopped
choices.why: `parseInt` returned nothing: it threw.

choices.text: Nothing caught the exception, so it left `main` and ended the thread
choices.why: Right: exit status 1, and every line after the throw was skipped.

prompt: Put the frames of `Fine.java`'s stack trace in the order they were printed, ignoring the `java.base` ones.
hint: Most recent first.

prompt: `Desk.java` ran four values through `perBook`. Which handled `"0"`?
hint: Dividing by zero is not a parsing problem.

choices.text: The `NumberFormatException` block, since `0` is a bad number of books
choices.why: `"0"` parses perfectly; the failure came at the division.

choices.text: The `ArithmeticException` block, printing `/ by zero`
choices.why: Right: integer division by zero throws `ArithmeticException`.

choices.text: Nothing, and the loop stopped there
choices.why: The loop went on and printed `2 -> 300` after it.

choices.text: Both blocks, one after the other
choices.why: Only the first matching `catch` runs.

prompt: A colleague wraps the whole of `main` in `try { ... } catch (Exception e) {}` so that the program "never crashes". What does section 02 suggest is wrong with it?
hint: Catch what you expected.

choices.text: It catches what nobody expected, and throws away the stack trace that would have explained it
choices.why: Right: for the unexpected, the stack trace is better than any handling, and an empty block is none.

choices.text: It does not compile, because `Exception` is too general to catch
choices.why: It compiles; catching `Exception` is legal, and that is the danger.

choices.text: It makes the program slower on every line
choices.why: A `try` costs next to nothing when nothing is thrown; the problem is what it hides.

prompt: A single `catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e)` that handles two classes is called a ___.
hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.

prompt: What does `e.getMessage()` return for the `NumberFormatException` of `"four"`?
hint: The transcript printed it after `not a number:`.

choices.text: The whole stack trace, as one string
choices.why: That is what `printStackTrace` writes; the message is one line.

choices.text: `NumberFormatException`, the class's name
choices.why: The class name comes before the colon in a stack trace; the message is what follows it.

choices.text: `For input string: "four"`
choices.why: Right: the text after the colon in a stack trace.

prompt: Why did the first `Count.java` not compile?
hint: Read the error to its end.

choices.text: Because `loans.txt` did not exist yet
choices.why: The compiler does not look for the file; the program failed on that later, at run time.

choices.text: `IOException` is checked, and `main` neither caught nor declared it
choices.why: Right: `must be caught or declared to be thrown`.

choices.text: Because `Files.readString` is not in `java.lang` and was not imported
choices.why: `Files` and `Path` were imported; the error named an unreported exception.

prompt: After `throws IOException` was added, `java Count` failed with `NoSuchFileException`. What was wrong with the program?
hint: What did the declaration say might happen?

choices.text: The declaration was in the wrong place and should be on `readString`
choices.why: `readString` already declares it; `main` was the method that had to choose.

choices.text: Nothing: it did what it declared, and the file was missing
choices.why: Right: once `loans.txt` existed, it printed `3 loans`.

choices.text: Declaring `throws` turns a compile error into a run-time error
choices.why: It turns an undecided case into a decided one; the file was really missing.

prompt: How many frames of the `NoSuchFileException` stack trace were inside the JDK, starting with `java.base/`?
hint: Every `at` line but the last.

prompt: Match each exception to its kind.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

prompt: Why is `IOException` checked while `NumberFormatException` is not?
hint: Could a correct program avoid each one?

choices.text: Because input and output are slower, and the compiler wants them visible
choices.why: Speed is not the criterion; whether a correct program can avoid it is.

choices.text: A correct program still meets a missing file; it never has to pass `"ten"` to `parseInt`
choices.why: Right: checked is for conditions outside the program, unchecked for mistakes in it.

choices.text: Because `NumberFormatException` was added to Java after checked exceptions were abolished
choices.why: Both are as old as the JDK, and checked exceptions were never abolished.

choices.text: Because `IOException` cannot be caught, only declared
choices.why: It can be caught; the compiler offered both choices.

prompt: Which classes are unchecked? Pick the description the section's table gives.
hint: Two branches of `Throwable`.

choices.text: Every exception thrown by the JDK itself
choices.why: `Files.readString` is the JDK, and its `IOException` is checked.

choices.text: `RuntimeException`, `Error` and their subclasses
choices.why: Right: every other `Exception` is checked.

choices.text: Exceptions whose names end in `Error`
choices.why: Names are a convention; the rule is the class each one extends.

prompt: In `lend("Dune")`, when did `close the ledger` print relative to the `return "lent"`?
hint: `lent` was printed by the caller.

choices.text: Never: `return` leaves the method at once
choices.why: It printed: a `return` waits for the `finally`.

choices.text: Before `lend Dune`
choices.why: The `try` ran first; `finally` runs as control leaves it.

choices.text: After the `return` was evaluated, before the method actually returned
choices.why: Right: `close the ledger` came between `lend Dune` and `lent`.

prompt: `lend(" ")` threw. In what order did `close the ledger` and `caught: no title` print, and why?
hint: The exception has to leave `lend` before `main` can catch it.

choices.text: `close the ledger` first: the `finally` ran as the exception left `lend`
choices.why: Right: then the exception reached `main`'s `catch`.

choices.text: `caught: no title` first: the `catch` runs before any `finally`
choices.why: The `catch` was in `main`; `lend`'s `finally` ran before the exception got there.

choices.text: Only `caught: no title`: a `finally` is skipped when there is an exception
choices.why: Running on that route is exactly what `finally` is for.

prompt: `swallow()` threw `IllegalStateException` and the program printed `all fine`. What happened to the exception?
hint: What was leaving the method when the `finally` returned?

choices.text: It was printed to the error stream, out of sight
choices.why: Both streams reach the terminal, and nothing was printed.

choices.text: It was caught by `main` and ignored
choices.why: `main` had no `catch` around `swallow()`.

choices.text: The `return` in `finally` replaced it, and it vanished
choices.why: Right: no stack trace and no message, which is why a `finally` must not `return`.

prompt: On which of these ways out does a `finally` block run? Choose all that apply.
hint: Every way the method ends, not every way the program does.

choices.text: The `try` reaches its end
choices.why: Yes: the ordinary way out.

choices.text: A `return` inside the `try`
choices.why: Yes: `close the ledger` printed before `lent`.

choices.text: An exception thrown inside the `try` and not caught there
choices.why: Yes: it ran while `no title` was on its way to `main`.

choices.text: `System.exit(0)` inside the `try`
choices.why: No: the JVM stopped, and `this line never prints` never printed.

prompt: What exit status did `Always.java` end with, after `System.exit(0)`?
hint: The last line of the transcript.

prompt: A method parses a member number typed at the desk and looks the member up in a file. Which exceptions should it make its callers deal with?
hint: Which failure can a correct program still meet?

choices.text: Neither: it should catch both and return `null`
choices.why: Returning `null` hides the failure from every caller, who then has to guess what happened.

choices.text: The `IOException` from the file, declared; a bad number is handled where it is typed
choices.why: Right: the file is outside the program, and the typing is best checked at the desk.

choices.text: Only `NumberFormatException`, since users mistype more often than disks fail
choices.why: Frequency does not decide it; the compiler's rule is about what a correct program can avoid.

prompt: A method declares `throws IOException` and its caller does neither catch nor declare it. What happens?
hint: The same rule applies to every caller in turn.

choices.text: The caller does not compile
choices.why: Right: the duty passes up, and each method must catch or declare.

choices.text: It compiles, and the exception is ignored if it happens
choices.why: The compiler refuses it: unreported exception.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning that can be suppressed
choices.why: It is an error, not a warning, for a checked exception.
